newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram concedes loss of presidency.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram concedes loss of presidency.

text.p: Abdala Bucaram finally conceded defeat in Ecuador's presidential crisis on Sunday, saying he had been deposed in a "congressional coup" that was backed by the country's armed forces.

Bucaram's dramatic statement, in a television interview broadcast before dawn, marked his first concession of defeat since Congress dismissed him as president three days earlier in a no-confidence vote citing alleged mental incompentence.

"Ecuador is going to be a disaster and I can assure you that the people will ask me to return within a month and a half," Bucaram said in the interview with Ecuavisa television from his home in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil.

"This is something unheard of in history," he added, referring to an agreement worked out between lawmakers and the country's powerful military leaders late on Saturday clearing the way for an end to the country's deepening constitutional crisis.

Lawmakers and military leaders agreed on a plan allowing Vice President Rosalia Arteaga to take over as interim president, but congressional leader Fabian Alarcon, who was initially voted by Congress to replace Bucaram, was expected to be re-appointed acting president within a matter of days.
"This is the dictatorship of the national Congress," Bucaram said, adding that while he remained the country's duly elected president he had effectively been stripped of all ability to rule.

Accusing the militiary of having "intervened politically" in national affairs, he said the "congressional coup" that sounded a death knell for his six-month-old government was certain to shake international confidence in Ecuador's democratic institutions and backfire on all those who had supported it.

His embittered remarks followed the resignation of his defence minister early on Saturday and a subsequent statement from a respected army general confirming that the military no longer considered Bucaram Ecuador's legitimate commander-in-chief.

Bucaram, known as "El Loco," or "madman", was ousted by Congress during a crippling strike that shut down Ecuador for two days last week in protest against hard economic austerity measures imposed by a president who had run as a candidate of an overwhelming majority of the poor.

"The armed forces have decided not to support Bucaram," said Gen. Jose Grijalva, commander of the army's 7th military zone, based in the southern province of Loja. "We are no longer taking orders from Bucaram, since he is no longer in charge and was dismissed by the National Congress," said Grijalva, who spoke in an interview with Radio Centinela.

The constitutional crisis that erupted after Bucaram's ouster stemmed not only from the fact that Bucaram himself refused to step down, but from claims by Arteaga and Alarcon that both had legal rights to succeeed him.
Alarcon was appointed president by fellow lawmakers on the same night that Bucaram was voted out.

The deal ending the crisis, announced on the floor of Congress after an extraordinary session early on Sunday, sees Arteaga take over immediately as interim president. But her rule will be short-lived as Alarcon is expected to assume full presidential power later in the week.

His appointment -- to serve until August 1998 -- would come only after lawmakers plugged a key loophole in the constitution that failed to spell out who replaces a sitting president, congressional officials said.
Arteaga was guaranteed a job as vice president until August 1998.
